```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(SMSD)
# Three decimal places for numbers written into the text.
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
```

## Why Study a Design First

In a sequential procedure the final sample size is not chosen; it is
whatever the data make it. The same is true of the width of the final
confidence interval, which never exceeds the target but can fall below
it, and of whether that interval contains the population value. Theory
describes these only in the limit. As the target width narrows, the
final sample size approaches the one a planner who knew the population
values would have fixed in advance, and the coverage of the interval
approaches the confidence level (Kelley, Darku, & Chattopadhyay, 2018,
Lemma 3 and Theorem 2; 2019, Theorem 1). A particular study is not at
the limit. A sensitivity analysis shows what the procedure does for one
population value, one target, and one way of checking, by running the
whole procedure many times on simulated data whose population value is
known.

DMAR pairs most of its `ss_aipe_*()` fixed sample size planners with a
sensitivity function (`ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity()` beside
`ss_aipe_smd()`, for example), which shows what happens when a planning
value is wrong. A
sequential procedure has no planning value. Its sensitivity analysis
shows what the stopping rule does in samples of the size the rule
itself produces.

## What Can Be Studied

```{r functions}
grep("^seq_.*_sensitivity$", ls("package:SMSD"), value = TRUE)
```

Every sequential AIPE procedure has a sensitivity function, the
contrast and the squared multiple correlation included; the one for the
correlation studies the Pearson coefficient. The two minimum risk
procedures, `seq_mr_cv()` and `seq_mr_smd()`, have one each, and so does
the budget constrained procedure. The classical procedures for a mean
have none; the section [A Population of Your
Own](#a-population-of-your-own) shows how to write the loop by hand,
which is also the way to study Kendall's tau, Spearman's rho, or a
population that the built in choices do not cover.

Each function does what a study would do: it draws the pilot sample,
checks the stopping rule, adds observations, and checks again, until
the rule is met. It does this `G` times and returns a summary.

## One Call

A training program is to be compared with a control group, and the
researcher wants a 95% confidence interval for the standardized mean
difference. What should a study with a target width of 0.80 expect if
the population value is 0.5?

```{r one-call}
smd <- seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 0.80, G = 100,
                                seed = 113)
smd
```

```{r one-call-values, include = FALSE}
n_known <- 4 * qnorm(0.975)^2 / 0.80^2 * (2 + 0.5^2 / 4)
```

The rows are the same for every `seq_aipe_*_sensitivity()` function.

* `true_value`, `target_width`, `conf_level`, `replications`: what was
  asked for.
* `mean_n`, `median_n`, `sd_n`: the final sample size, per group for
  this effect size. A study like this one ends with about
  `r round(smd$value[smd$term == "mean_n"])` per group, give or take a
  few. With
  the population values known, the sample size for this width would be
  `4 * qnorm(0.975)^2 / 0.80^2 * (2 + 0.5^2 / 4)` =
  `r round(n_known, 1)` per group for normal data, so the procedure
  spends almost nothing for not knowing them.
* `mean_width`, `median_width`, `pct_width_within`: the width of the
  final interval, and the percentage of replications in which it was no
  wider than the target. That percentage is 100 whenever the stopping
  rule ended every replication.
* `coverage`: the proportion of final intervals that contained the
  population value.
* `pct_hit_max_n`: the percentage of replications that the cap `max_n`
  (100,000 by default) stopped before the rule was met. When it is
  above zero the other rows describe a truncated procedure.
* `pct_variance_unusable`: the percentage of replications in which, at
  one or more checks, the variance estimate was zero, negative, or not
  finite, so that the rule was reported as not met there and sampling
  continued (`vignette("seq-aipe-smd", package = "SMSD")` shows such a
  check).

The result is an object of class `smsd_sensitivity`. It prints every
value in fixed notation, and it is an ordinary data frame with columns
`term` and `value`, so a number can be taken out by name. The one line
function `value_of()` defined here does that in the rest of this
vignette.

```{r one-call-object}
class(smd)
smd$value[smd$term == "coverage"]

value_of <- function(out, term) out$value[out$term == term]
value_of(smd, "mean_n")
```

Every row is an estimate from `G` replications. The Monte Carlo
standard error of a coverage of <em>p</em> is the square root of
<em>p</em>(1 &minus; <em>p</em>) / <em>G</em>:

```{r one-call-se}
mc_se <- function(out) {
  p <- value_of(out, "coverage")
  G <- value_of(out, "replications")
  sqrt(p * (1 - p) / G)
}
mc_se(smd)
```

With `G = 100` the coverage above is known only to within about two
standard errors, `r f3(2 * mc_se(smd))`, either way. The runs in this
vignette use a small `G` and wide targets so that it builds in seconds.
Unless the text gives a standard error and draws a conclusion from it,
they show how to read the output and are not evidence about the
procedures. A result that will be reported deserves `G = 10000`, at the
width the study will use, which puts the standard error of a coverage
near 0.95 at about 0.002. At a narrow target such a run can take from
minutes to an hour or more, and nothing is printed while it runs, so
time a call with a small `G` first. The time grows with the final sample
size and falls as `batch` rises, but a larger `batch` describes a study
that checks less often ([Checking in Batches](#checking-in-batches)), so
use the batch size the study will use. The `seed` argument makes a run
reproducible and leaves the caller's random number stream as it found
it.

Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, pp. 232--233, Tables 1 and 2)
report simulations of this kind for the standardized mean difference,
with one observation per group added at each stage and 5,000
replications, under the heading "Characteristics of the final sample
size: An empirical demonstration."

The other functions are called the same way, with two exceptions that
follow from what they study. `seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity()` also takes the
number of predictors, `p`, and is used below.
`seq_aipe_c_sensitivity()` has no single population value to be given:
it takes the population means of the groups, the contrast weights, and
the population standard deviations (1 by default), and its `true_value`
row is the contrast of the means. Here a new training format is
compared with the average of two existing ones, the population contrast
is half a standard deviation, and the target width is 1:

```{r contrast}
contrast <- seq_aipe_c_sensitivity(true_means = c(0.5, 0, 0),
                                   contrast_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),
                                   width = 1, G = 100, seed = 113)
contrast
```

The sample sizes in this summary are per group, and the width of a
contrast is in the units of the response. The coverage row again rests
on 100 replications; its standard error is
`r f3(mc_se(contrast))`.

## Checking in Batches

By default the stopping rule is checked after every observation (per
group, for a two group design), which is the purely sequential procedure
of the articles. Few studies can do that. The `batch` argument is the
number of observations added between checks, and a sensitivity analysis
shows what checking less often costs.

```{r batch}
batches <- c(10, 20)
runs <- lapply(batches, function(b) {
  seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 0.80, G = 100,
                           seed = 113, batch = b)
})
runs <- c(list(smd), runs)

overshoot <- sapply(runs, function(out) {
  c(mean_n = value_of(out, "mean_n"),
    mean_width = value_of(out, "mean_width"),
    coverage = value_of(out, "coverage"),
    se_coverage = mc_se(out))
})
colnames(overshoot) <- paste("batch", c(1, batches))
round(overshoot, 3)
```

A study that checks only after every batch cannot stop between checks,
so it ends with more observations and a somewhat narrower interval.
Here the mean final sample size per group rises from
`r formatC(overshoot["mean_n", 1], format = "f", digits = 1)` with a
check after every observation to
`r formatC(overshoot["mean_n", 3], format = "f", digits = 1)` with a
check after every 20. The coverage row cannot separate the three
designs: its entries differ by at most
`r f3(diff(range(overshoot["coverage", ])))`, and each has a Monte Carlo
standard error of `r f3(min(overshoot["se_coverage", ]))` to
`r f3(max(overshoot["se_coverage", ]))` (the last row). In larger runs
at a target width of 0.4 the mean
final sample size per group was 199.1, 201.2, 203.6, and 209.5 for
batches of 1, 5, 10, and 20, about half a batch more per group, and
coverage stayed between 0.949 and 0.952 (4,700 to 6,000 replications
each; `?seq_aipe_sensitivity`).

## Reading the Coverage Row

The width of the final interval is guaranteed. Its coverage is not: the
articles prove that coverage approaches the confidence level as the
target narrows, and say nothing about any particular width. Whether a
target is narrow enough depends on the effect size, on the population
value, and on the distribution of the data.

For a standardized mean difference of 0.5 and normal data, even the
wide target used above is narrow enough: with many more replications
the coverage at a width of 0.8 was 0.95 (`?seq_aipe_sensitivity`; the
row is in the table below). The same design with right skewed data is
a different matter. The argument `distribution = "skewed"` draws both
groups from a chi square distribution with 3 degrees of freedom,
shifted and scaled so that the means and the variance are those of the
normal case. This run checks after every five participants per group,
which keeps 1,000 replications quick:

```{r skewed}
skewed <- seq_aipe_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, width = 0.80,
                                   distribution = "skewed", G = 1000,
                                   seed = 113, batch = 5)
round(c(mean_n = value_of(skewed, "mean_n"),
        coverage = value_of(skewed, "coverage"),
        se_coverage = mc_se(skewed)), 3)
```

```{r skewed-values, include = FALSE}
cov_skewed <- value_of(skewed, "coverage")
short_skewed <- (0.95 - cov_skewed) / mc_se(skewed)
```

The coverage is `r f3(cov_skewed)`, which is
`r formatC(abs(short_skewed), format = "f", digits = 1)` standard errors
`r if (short_skewed > 0) "below" else "above"` the 0.95 that was asked
for`r if (short_skewed > 2) ", more than Monte Carlo error accounts for" else ""`.
The interval is as narrow as requested, but it contains the population
value somewhat less often than its confidence level says.

```{r skewed-narrow, include = FALSE}
tour <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "aipe_simulation_results.rds",
                            package = "SMSD"))
tour_smd <- tour$summary[tour$summary$method ==
                           "Standardized mean difference" &
                           tour$summary$width == 0.4, ]
tour_k <- tour_smd$coverage[tour_smd$distribution == "skewed"]
tour_n <- tour_smd$coverage[tour_smd$distribution == "normal"]
stopifnot(length(tour_k) == 3, length(tour_n) == 3)
```

At narrower targets the shortfall under skew is much smaller, though at
a width of 0.4 it has not vanished: coverage was 0.944 at a width of 0.4
and 0.949 at 0.2, against 0.952 and 0.946 for normal data
(`?seq_aipe_smd`). The verification study in
`vignette("complete-tour", package = "SMSD")`, with
`r formatC(tour$meta$G, format = "d", big.mark = ",")` replications for
each of the population values 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 at a width of 0.4,
found `r f3(min(tour_k))` to `r f3(max(tour_k))` for skewed data and
`r f3(min(tour_n))` to `r f3(max(tour_n))` for normal data: about half a
percentage point short of 0.95 under skew, which is more than Monte
Carlo error.
<!-- not from a help page: 0.8 -->

In the other direction, coverage is lower again at a target wider
still, for normal data as well, and the more so the larger the
population value. A design at the wide end deserves a run of its own
under each population that is plausible.

For a correlation, a target half as wide as the one above may not be
narrow enough even with normal data. This study of a correlation of 0.4
checks after every five pairs:

```{r coverage}
r <- seq_aipe_r_sensitivity(true_value = 0.4, width = 0.4, G = 100,
                            seed = 113, batch = 5)
r
```

In this run `r round(100 * value_of(r, "coverage"))` of the 100 final
intervals contained the population correlation, a coverage of
`r f3(value_of(r, "coverage"))` with a standard error of
`r f3(mc_se(r))` where 0.95 was asked for, and in
`r round(value_of(r, "pct_variance_unusable"))` percent of the
replications the variance estimate was unusable at some check. A run of
this size cannot give the second decimal place, but the shortfall is
real: with one pair added at a time and many more replications, the
coverage at this population value and width is 0.78 (the third row of
the table below). The reason is the estimate of
the asymptotic variance in small samples. It is a combination of ratios
of sample moments that tends to run low when the sample is small, so the
rule is met too early and the interval is too narrow (Kelley, Darku, &
Chattopadhyay, 2019, Appendix D, p. 514).
<!-- figures from `?seq_aipe_sensitivity` -->

The table collects what these functions measured for the standardized
mean difference and for some of the harder cases, at a 95% confidence
level with the default settings and normal data unless a distribution
is named. It is taken from `?seq_aipe_sensitivity`, where the
replication counts and standard errors are given (each row rests on
800 to 34,000 replications).

| Effect size and population value | Target width | Mean final n | Coverage | Percent of replications with an unusable variance estimate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standardized mean difference, 0.5 | 0.8 | 51 | 0.95 | below 0.1 |
| Standardized mean difference, 0.5 | 0.4 | 199 | 0.95 | 0.0 |
| Correlation, 0.4 | 0.4 | 55 | 0.78 | 16.5 |
| Correlation, 0.4 | 0.2 | 263 | 0.93 | 0.9 |
| Correlation, 0.4 | 0.1 | 1,079 | 0.95 | 0.0 |
| Correlation, 0.9 | 0.1 | 75 | 0.45 | 79.5 |
| Correlation, 0.9 | 0.025 | 819 | 0.90 | 1.3 |
| Regression slope, 0.5 | 0.4 | 80 | 0.83 | 20.1 |
| Regression slope, 0.5 | 0.2 | 377 | 0.94 | 1.3 |
| Regression slope, 2 | 0.2 | 217 | 0.61 | 65.3 |
| Coefficient of variation, 0.5, lognormal | 0.2 | 62 | 0.79 | 0.0 |
| Coefficient of variation, 0.5, lognormal | 0.05 | 1,561 | 0.90 | 0.0 |
| Gini index, 0.3 | 0.2 | 30 | 0.89 | 0.0 |

Three things in the table matter for planning.

First, coverage depends on the population value as well as on the
width. A width of 0.1 is ample for a correlation of 0.4 and far from
enough for a correlation of 0.9, because a strong correlation is
estimated with so little sampling error that the rule is met in a small
sample. Run the analysis at every population value that is plausible
for the study, the strongest included.

Second, the remedies are a narrower target, a larger minimum pilot
sample (`m_0`), or both. With `m_0 = 40` at a width of 0.4, coverage for
a correlation of 0.4 rose from 0.78 to 0.90 while the mean final sample
size rose from 55 to 64, and coverage for a slope of 0.5 rose from 0.83
to 0.92. A larger pilot is a weaker remedy when the relationship is
strong: for a correlation of 0.9 at a width of 0.1, `m_0 = 100` raised
coverage only from 0.45 to 0.69.
<!-- figures from `?seq_aipe_sensitivity` -->

Third, an unusable variance estimate at an early check is not the
problem itself; the check functions report the rule as not met there
and sampling continues. It is a sign that the samples the rule is
working with are small for this effect size, and the estimate on which
a replication finally stops can still be too low. When the relationship
is very strong the estimate can also stay unusable for a long time, so
set `max_n` when exploring such conditions and read `pct_hit_max_n`.

## Several Conditions in One Table: The Squared Multiple Correlation

The summaries are data frames, so a table over conditions takes a few
lines. For the squared multiple correlation the condition that matters
most is the number of predictors. The function generates multivariate
normal data, the assumption under which that procedure is derived; `p`
is the number of predictors.

```{r r2}
predictors <- c(2, 5, 10)
r2_runs <- lapply(predictors, function(p) {
  seq_aipe_R2_sensitivity(true_value = 0.50, width = 0.30, p = p, G = 200,
                          seed = 113)
})
data.frame(
  predictors = predictors,
  mean_n = sapply(r2_runs, value_of, "mean_n"),
  coverage = sapply(r2_runs, value_of, "coverage"),
  se_coverage = sapply(r2_runs, mc_se)
)
```

The stopping rule asks for no more observations when there are more
predictors, and the coverage falls: the sample squared multiple
correlation overestimates the population value by more the more
predictors there are, and the rule does not correct for it. The standard errors
in the last column are large because `G` is small, but the trend is not
a Monte Carlo accident. With 10,000 replications per condition the
coverage at this population value and width was 0.900 with 2
predictors, 0.845 with 5, 0.668 with 10, and 0.361 with 15
(`?seq_aipe_R2`). `vignette("seq-aipe-correlations", package = "SMSD")`
discusses what to do about it.

## Minimum Risk

The minimum risk procedures (Chattopadhyay & Kelley, 2016, 2017) have no
interval and no coverage. Their sensitivity functions compare the
procedure with the best fixed sample size, the one that would minimize
the risk if the population value were known. For a standardized mean difference of 0.5, a price of 8,000 per
unit of squared error, and a cost of 4 per participant:

```{r mr}
mr <- seq_mr_smd_sensitivity(true_value = 0.5, A = 8000, c = 4, G = 200,
                             seed = 113)
mr
```

The rows to read are `ratio_n1` and `ratio_n2`, the mean final sample
size of each group over the optimal one, and `risk_efficiency`, the
mean realized loss over the minimum risk, with its Monte Carlo standard
error in the next row. Each should be near 1. Here the procedure takes
about `r round(100 * (value_of(mr, "ratio_n1") - 1))` percent more than
the optimal `r round(value_of(mr, "optimal_n1"), 1)` per group, because
the correction term in its stopping rule guards against stopping too
early, and its risk efficiency is `r f3(value_of(mr, "risk_efficiency"))`
(standard error `r f3(value_of(mr, "se_risk_efficiency"))`): the risk is
nearly flat around its minimum, so the extra observations cost little.
`seq_mr_cv_sensitivity()` reports the same quantities for the
coefficient of variation, with one row where the two group function
has two: `cost`, `optimal_n`, `mean_n`, `median_n`, `sd_n`, and
`ratio_n`. Both functions take `batch`.

## A Budget

`seq_budget_sensitivity()` runs the budget constrained procedure of
Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025) for
population means, standard deviations, costs, and a budget that the
user supplies. It adds one observation at a time to the group that
`seq_budget_next()` names, so it has no `batch` argument. Here a new
training format is compared with the average of two existing ones; the
population contrast is 2, and a noninferiority margin of 5 is of
interest.

```{r budget}
budget <- seq_budget_sensitivity(
  true_means = c(52, 50, 50),
  true_sds = c(9, 6, 6),
  contrast_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),
  cost_per_group = c(38, 15, 10),
  budget = 1500,
  margin = 5,
  G = 200,
  seed = 113,
  m_0 = 10
)
budget
```

The summary answers the questions a budget raises. How much of it is
spent: `mean_total_cost`, and `pct_within_budget`, which is 100 by
construction. How sampling ends: `pct_rule_met` is the percentage of
replications in which every group reached its criterion, and in the
rest the budget could not pay for another needed observation, which is
the usual ending. How close the allocation comes to the best one: the
`mean_n_` rows beside the `optimal_n_` rows, and `mean_true_variance`
beside `optimal_variance`. How well the interval and the test perform:
`coverage`, with a standard error here of `r f3(mc_se(budget))`, and
`noninferiority_rejection_rate`, which is the power of the
noninferiority test at this margin because the population contrast is
above the negative of the margin.

## A Population of Your Own

The sensitivity functions generate data from a few named populations.
When the population of interest is not among them, or the procedure has
no sensitivity function, the loop is short to write, because the check
functions do all of the work. The example is a standardized mean
difference between two groups rated on a 7 point scale: discrete,
bounded, and skewed in opposite directions in the two groups.

```{r own}
p_control <- c(0.10, 0.20, 0.25, 0.20, 0.12, 0.08, 0.05)
p_program <- rev(p_control)

rating_mean <- function(p) sum(1:7 * p)
rating_var <- function(p) sum((1:7 - rating_mean(p))^2 * p)
true_delta <- (rating_mean(p_program) - rating_mean(p_control)) /
  sqrt((rating_var(p_program) + rating_var(p_control)) / 2)
true_delta

one_study <- function(width = 0.80, batch = 10) {
  m <- seq_aipe_smd_pilot(width = width)
  program <- sample(7, m, replace = TRUE, prob = p_program)
  control <- sample(7, m, replace = TRUE, prob = p_control)
  repeat {
    out <- seq_aipe_smd(program, control, width = width)
    if (attr(out, "is_satisfied")) break
    program <- c(program, sample(7, batch, replace = TRUE, prob = p_program))
    control <- c(control, sample(7, batch, replace = TRUE, prob = p_control))
  }
  summary(out)
}

set.seed(113)
studies <- do.call(rbind, replicate(100, one_study(), simplify = FALSE))
covered <- with(studies, lower_limit <= true_delta & true_delta <= upper_limit)
c(mean_n = mean(studies$current_n), coverage = mean(covered))
```

`summary()` turns each final check into one row, so the replications
stack into a data frame with one row per simulated study. The coverage
of `r f3(mean(covered))` rests on 100 studies and has a standard error
of about `r f3(sqrt(mean(covered) * (1 - mean(covered)) / 100))`. A
loop for Kendall's tau or Spearman's rho through `seq_aipe_r()` has the
same shape.

So does a loop for a classical procedure, none of which has a
sensitivity function. The purely sequential fixed width interval for a
normal mean, `seq_fwd_norm_mean()`, takes the half width `d`. With a
half width of 0.5 and a population standard deviation of 2, a planner
who knew the standard deviation would take
(`qnorm(0.975) * 2 / 0.5`)<sup>2</sup> =
`r formatC((qnorm(0.975) * 2 / 0.5)^2, format = "f", digits = 1)`
observations.

```{r own-classical}
one_mean_study <- function(d = 0.5, mu = 10, sigma = 2) {
  x <- rnorm(seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d = d), mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  repeat {
    out <- seq_fwd_norm_mean(x, d = d)
    if (attr(out, "is_satisfied")) break
    x <- c(x, rnorm(1, mean = mu, sd = sigma))
  }
  summary(out)
}

set.seed(113)
mean_studies <- do.call(rbind, replicate(100, one_mean_study(),
                                         simplify = FALSE))
mean_covered <- with(mean_studies, lower_limit <= 10 & 10 <= upper_limit)
c(mean_n = mean(mean_studies$current_n), coverage = mean(mean_covered))
```

```{r own-classical-values, include = FALSE}
mean_cov <- mean(mean_covered)
mean_cov_se <- sqrt(mean_cov * (1 - mean_cov) / nrow(mean_studies))
```

The `r nrow(mean_studies)` studies ended with
`r formatC(mean(mean_studies$current_n), format = "f", digits = 1)`
observations on average, and `r f3(mean_cov)` of their intervals
contained the population mean (standard error `r f3(mean_cov_se)`).
The confidence level of this procedure is asymptotic, and a shortfall at
a sample size of this order is real: for the same design
`?seq_fwd_norm_mean` reports a coverage of 0.938 from 40,000
replications where 0.95 was asked for. A run of this size cannot
measure a shortfall of one percentage point; it shows the shape of the
loop. The help pages of the classical procedures report runs of this
kind with tens of thousands of replications, and
`vignette("special-cases-and-simulation", package = "SMSD")` collects
them.

## Practical Guidance

* Run the analysis at the width, confidence level, pilot size, and
  batch size the study will use, at every population value that is
  plausible, and under a skewed population as well as a normal one where
  the function offers the choice.
* Use `G = 10000` for anything that will be reported, give the seed,
  and report the Monte Carlo standard error with the coverage. Time the
  call with a small `G` first: at a narrow target ten thousand
  replications can take an hour or more.
* Read `coverage` before relying on an interval at a planned width, and
  `pct_hit_max_n` before reading anything else when `max_n` was set.
* When coverage is short of the confidence level, plan a narrower
  target, raise `m_0`, or both, and run the analysis again.
* A preregistration or a proposal is the place for the resulting table:
  it tells a reviewer how large the study is likely to become and what
  the interval at the end can be trusted to do.
